causalMechanism.primaryVector: Chronic gastroesophageal reflux causes Barrett's esophagus by driving reparative metaplasia of the distal esophageal epithelium: repeated exposure of the squamous mucosa to gastric acid and pepsin (and, where present, bile) produces chronic epithelial injury, and in genetically susceptible individuals the healing response replaces the damaged squamous epithelium with intestinalized columnar mucosa — the metaplastic change that defines Barrett's esophagus and that carries the risk of progression through low-grade and high-grade dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma. The risk is not binary: longer duration and greater frequency of reflux symptoms, male sex, older age, central obesity, smoking, and family history all raise the probability of the metaplastic transformation, and screening guidelines treat GERD as the cardinal clinical criterion. The quantitative evidence is direct: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 studies (12,883 patients with GERD and 51,350 without) found Barrett's esophagus prevalence of 7% (95% CI 5.8-8.5%) in patients with GERD versus 2.2% (95% CI 1.6-3%) in those without, with an odds ratio for Barrett's esophagus of 2.91 (95% CI 2.06-4.11) and 4.17 (95% CI 1.78-9.77) for long-segment disease; a systematic review and meta-analysis of 49 studies and 307,273 individuals found Barrett's prevalence rising from 0.8% in the low-risk general population to 3% with GERD and 12.2% with GERD plus any additional risk factor, with a positive linear relationship between the number of risk factors and prevalence; and the JAMA scientific review of the reflux-Barrett's-adenocarcinoma sequence documents that Barrett's esophagus — metaplasia from squamous to intestinalized columnar mucosa — is associated with chronic reflux and is the pathway through which adenocarcinoma develops. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), Barrett's esophagus developing in a veteran with service-connected GERD is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the GERD diagnosis (duration, symptom frequency and severity, endoscopic and, where performed, ambulatory pH findings), the upper endoscopy with biopsy demonstrating intestinal metaplasia and any dysplasia grade, and the chronology of chronic reflux relative to the metaplastic change; and address competing contributors — obesity and central adiposity, smoking, age and male sex as susceptibility factors rather than alternative diagnoses, and the known inverse association with Helicobacter pylori. Where Barrett's esophagus or dysplasia is documented before the service-connected reflux disease, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. Where the veteran's GERD itself is evaluated under DC 7206, § 4.14 prohibits using the same stricture or dysphagia findings to evaluate both the GERD and the Barrett's esophagus.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Injury-repair causal sequence: repeated reflux exposure can cause esophagitis and ulcerative injury; healing of sustained injury can produce fibrotic scar and a fixed luminal narrowing, usually distal in a peptic stricture. The resulting mechanical resistance to bolus passage causes dysphagia and may require repeated dilation. This is a GERD → reflux esophagitis → peptic stricture pathway, not a claim that every episode of heartburn causes irreversible fibrosis. Pregun et al. (PMID 19439958) identifies peptic stricture as a consequence of GERD, emphasizes exclusion of malignancy, and explains why healing coexistent esophagitis and effective acid suppression reduce repeated dilation. In the 366-patient randomized trial by Smith et al. (PMID 7926495), omeprazole versus ranitidine after dilation reduced the proportion needing redilation at 12 months from 46% to 30% among the reported evaluable groups. This intervention evidence supports an ongoing acid-dependent contribution to recurrence; it does not prove the cause of all benign strictures or estimate an individual nexus probability. The ACG guideline (PMID 34807007) supplies an evidence-based GERD evaluation and management standard.

A prior clinical diagnosis of GERD without objective or persuasive longitudinal support is not enough to label a new narrowing 'peptic.' Competing causes in the differential include esophageal malignancy, eosinophilic esophagitis, caustic ingestion, radiation injury, anastomotic narrowing, and pill-induced injury. Achalasia and other motility disorders can cause dysphagia without a peptic fixed narrowing. A short distal scar with prior erosive reflux and an appropriate treatment history supports the route, whereas a proximal or multifocal lesion, eosinophilic histology, cancer, or a relevant alternative exposure may favor a different etiology.

Legal theory: when service-connected GERD produces the documented peptic stricture, the connection is causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), not a medication side effect. If an independently caused stricture predates GERD, any reflux-related increase in recurrent narrowing or dysphagia belongs to an independently reasoned § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis. Record baseline caliber, dilation frequency, diet tolerance, and clinical severity from pre-aggravation or qualifying earliest records, and distinguish natural progression of the original lesion. An 'at least as likely as not' conclusion requires the veteran-specific temporal, endoscopic, histologic, and differential evidence to be at least approximately balanced; population evidence and treatment response alone cannot supply that conclusion.

Rating and graph controls: current DC 7203 requires documented stricture findings and grades dysphagia/treatment burden; DC 7206 also uses stricture-related criteria. Establishing a distinct diagnosis does not automatically permit two ratings for the same dysphagia, dilation burden, or nutritional impairment under § 4.14. Claim-period-specific criteria must be checked rather than applying obsolete GERD-by-hiatal-hernia coding to every claim. The repository already carries esophagitis → esophageal-stricture → dysphagia. Preserve that intermediate-node physiology and perform a redundancy review before adding a direct GERD → stricture shortcut; source PMID 19439958 is already registered and requires provenance-aware reuse rather than a duplicate source entity.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Pharmacological sequence: metoclopramide is a dopamine-receptor antagonist (with 5-HT3 antagonism and 5-HT4 agonism) used as an antiemetic and gastroprokinetic; prolonged blockade of nigrostriatal and mesolimbic dopamine pathways can produce persistent involuntary choreoathetoid movements of the tongue, face, jaw and extremities — tardive dyskinesia — after prolonged exposure. Al-Saffar et al. (PMID 31050085) review this pharmacology, the regulatory restrictions introduced for long-term or high-dose oral use, and estimate the risk of tardive dyskinesia from metoclopramide at roughly 0.1 percent per 1,000 patient-years. Rao and Camilleri (PMID 19886950), reviewing the literature after the FDA's 2009 black-box warning, concluded the risk is likely below 1 percent — materially lower than the 1-10 percent previously suggested in national guidelines — and note that risk may be modified by age, dose, duration and pharmacokinetic/pharmacogenetic factors such as DRD3 and cytochrome P450 variation. Kenney et al. (PMID 18223146) identify metoclopramide as an increasingly recognized cause of tardive dyskinesia. These sources establish a recognized iatrogenic cause with a low absolute incidence; they do not quantify any particular veteran's risk, and the literature cannot identify in advance which exposed patients will develop persistent movements.

Competing causes include other dopamine-blocking agents (antipsychotics, promethazine, prochlorperazine), prior neuroleptic exposure, and underlying neurodegenerative disease. Because the same movement may be codable through several neurologic analogs, findings must be attributed once.

Legal and rating analysis: 'Medication Side Effect' is treatment-mediated secondary causation under § 3.310(a): service-connected GERD, through documented metoclopramide exposure, causes tardive dyskinesia. The GERD host file is published and does not currently propose this, and the tardive-dyskinesia identity already receives one association-only edge from bipolar disorder in which an antipsychotic is named as the proximate agent; this proposal is a distinct non-antipsychotic agent route and must be reconciled for duplicate scope rather than assumed additive. If a pre-existing movement disorder was worsened by therapy, analyze § 3.310(b) aggravation separately with a baseline and natural-course description. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion must weigh exposure chronology, persistence after withdrawal where safely documented, and competing causes against the low population incidence; a low base rate does not preclude an individual causal opinion, but it raises the evidentiary bar. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: there is no dedicated tardive-dyskinesia DC; §§ 4.20 and 4.27 require a justified analogous code selected from affected muscle groups and severity, with DC 8103 and DC 8004 as candidates only. Apply § 4.14 to avoid duplication with any mental-disorder or neurologic evaluation of the same movements.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Acid-mediated dissolution sequence: in service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease, gastroduodenal contents — hydrochloric acid at a pH frequently below 2 and the proteolytic enzyme pepsin — are regurgitated to the oropharynx, where they contact the palatal and occlusal surfaces of the teeth. Dental apatite dissolves once the local pH falls below its critical value (approximately 5.5 for hydroxyapatite), so repeated acid exposure produces irreversible, cumulative loss of enamel and then dentin rather than the reversible demineralization seen with dietary acid alone; the absence of normal salivary buffering and clearance during sleep amplifies overnight regurgitation, and reduced salivary flow can further slow re-hardening. Picos et al. (PMID 30564013), a systematic review of dental erosion in GERD, report erosive-lesion prevalence in GERD patients of about 48.81 percent versus 20.48 percent in non-GERD comparators, with a median prevalence near 25.5 percent and a reported range of 10.6 to 42 percent, and describe dental erosion as an extraesophageal complication of GERD. Ortiz et al. (PMID 33571021) systematically reviewed the association and prevalence of erosive wear in GERD and conclude that GERD can be considered a risk factor, while Alavi et al. (PMID 24738088) compared patients with and without GERD and found a higher risk of dental erosion in the GERD group in a sample of 140 adults aged 30 to 50. These sources establish reflux acid as a recognized cause of erosive tooth-surface loss at the mechanism and population level; they are observational, they do not quantify any individual veteran's exposure, and the literature cannot identify in advance which reflux patients will lose tooth substance.

These sources establish reflux acid as a recognized cause of erosive tooth-surface loss at the mechanism and population level; they are observational, they do not quantify any individual veteran's exposure, and the literature cannot identify in advance which reflux patients will lose tooth substance.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the reflux diagnosis and its objective confirmation (endoscopy, ambulatory pH or impedance testing, or a documented reflux regimen), the onset date of reflux relative to the dental changes, and a dental examination with intraoral photographs or casts describing lesion location and depth. Erosion attributable to reflux characteristically affects palatal surfaces of the maxillary anterior teeth and, in more advanced disease, occlusal surfaces and posterior teeth; dietary acid (citrus, carbonated drinks, vinegar, acidic sports or vitamin-C products), occupational acid exposure, bruxism/attrition, abrasive toothpaste technique, reduced salivary flow from anticholinergic or other xerogenic medication, and eating disorders with self-induced vomiting are competing causes that must be excluded or apportioned. An intrinsic-acid route from an eating disorder is an already-recognized alternative route into this same dental identity, which the catalog records as an association-only incoming edge from bulimia nervosa; a reflux attribution requires the acid source to be the documented reflux rather than covert vomiting. Chronology (reflux preceding the erosion), an anatomically consistent palatal distribution, absence of a competing dietary or occupational acid source, and objective reflux findings favor the reflux-related route; erosion that predates the reflux or tracks a dietary pattern weakens it.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected GERD and its acid regurgitation produce the tooth-surface loss and any resulting tooth loss; the theory is causation rather than aggravation because a new erosive process is being produced by the service-connected reflux. If a pre-existing erosive or abrasive lesion is asserted to have been worsened by reflux acid, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline (pre-reflux dental status or imaging) and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires reasoned balancing of the objective reflux findings, the palatal distribution, the exposure chronology and the exclusion of competing causes, because observational prevalence data alone do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here.
